title: How a level of my pixel art tower defense gets made: blockout → Nano Banana → scripts → Godot
author: maskfallgame
selftext:
This is how the first level of Maskfall (a pixel art tower defense for iPhone and Android, made in Godot) goes from idea to game. Small studio (solo) in Italy, alongside my day job.

First of all the idea, the reference images, the palette, the story etc.

Then:

**1. Blockout.** A script draws the level layout in flat colors: road, tower slots, river, buildings. Why: at first I gave Nano Banana a simple plan and it moved the roads and invented extra slots. A flat-color blockout plus "repaint this" keeps the measures.

**2. Nano Banana.** It repaints the blockout, with the first level's concept (the one I picked) as style reference and a small catalogue of our buildings. Also, a palette of colours is helpful.

**3. Our scripts.** They reduce each background to its own 64-color palette, cut out what stands up (houses, trees, the mill) so units walk behind it, bake the shadows and build the layers the game needs.

**4. Characters and towers.** Concept from Nano Banana, then PixelLab for sprites, poses and directions, then the same scripts clean palette, outlines and frames.

**5. Code.** Claude Code writes the game in Godot. Bots play the levels to help with balancing.

What didn't work:
- At first all the art was drawn with code only (8 rounds on the same bridge). Then I moved to generators.
- Assembling assets generated one by one looked off. One whole background generated at once works much better.

One question for you: how do you keep a consistent style across 17+ generated backgrounds?

Thanks for any suggestions.
